lead: Cut a loaded machine member anywhere and the section must carry an internal axial force P, shear force V, bending moment M and torque T. Each makes its own stress pattern: P a uniform normal stress, V a shear stress, M a normal stress that grows linearly from the neutral axis, and T a shear stress that grows from the shaft axis to the surface. The four formulas σ = P/A, τ = V/A, σ = My/I and τ = Tr/J size a first trial section for a shaft, pin, lever or bolt, and every later check in machine design builds on them.

sections.h3: Direct stresses: tension, compression and shear

blocks.text: σ is the direct normal stress (MPa = N/mm²); P is the axial force along the centroidal axis (N); A is the area resisting it (mm²). Tension is positive, compression negative. τ is the average shear stress (MPa); V is the shear force (N) and A the area that would slide.

The normal stress is uniform only away from load points, holes and grooves; near them the stress rises (stress concentration, see failure theories and fatigue design). Use the net area for a plate with a hole or the core area for a threaded rod. A pin that passes through a fork is in double shear: it must shear across two sections at once, so A = 2 × πd²/4.

A bending moment M (N·mm) stretches the fibres on one side of a beam and shortens those on the other. Between them lies the neutral axis, where the bending stress is zero; for pure bending it passes through the centroid of the section.

y is the distance of a fibre from the neutral axis (mm); I = ∫y² dA is the second moment of area (mm⁴); c is the distance to the outermost fibre (mm); Z = I/c is the section modulus (mm³). Rectangle b wide and h deep: I = bh³/12, Z = bh²/6. Solid circle of diameter d: I = πd⁴/64, Z = πd³/32.

The formula assumes a straight beam of linear elastic material, small deflections and plane sections that remain plane. A transverse shear force V also gives a shear stress across the section that is zero at the outer fibres and largest at the neutral axis: 1.5V/A for a rectangle and (4/3)V/A for a circle. It is usually small beside the bending stress except in short, deep members. In a deeply curved member the neutral axis shifts and the stress is no longer linear; see curved beams.
A torque T (N·mm) twists a circular shaft. Each cross-section rotates as a rigid disc, and the shear stress grows linearly from zero on the axis to its largest value at the surface.

r is the radial distance from the axis (mm), the same r over which J = ∫r² dA is taken; J is the polar second moment of area (mm⁴): πd⁴/32 for a solid shaft, π(d<sub>o</sub>⁴ − d<sub>i</sub>⁴)/32 for a hollow one with outer and inner diameters d<sub>o</sub> and d<sub>i</sub>. J/(d/2) = πd³/16 is the polar section modulus Z<sub>p</sub>. For a solid circle J = 2I.

A shaft transmitting power Pw (W) at N rpm carries T = 60Pw/(2πN) in N·m. Torsional stress is shear and bending stress is normal, so they cannot be added; they are combined through principal stresses in combined loading. Figure 1.6.1 draws the three stress patterns across the shaft of the first worked example.

examples.question: A 40 mm diameter solid shaft carries an axial compressive load of 30 kN, a bending moment of 600 N·m and a torque of 450 N·m. Find the direct stress, the maximum bending stress and the maximum torsional shear stress.
steps: Area: A = π × 40²/4 = 1256.6 mm². Direct stress: σ = 30,000/1256.6 = 23.87 MPa, compressive (−23.87 MPa).
Section modulus: Z = π × 40³/32 = 6283.2 mm³. Bending stress: σ<sub>b</sub> = 600,000/6283.2 = 95.49 MPa, tension on one side and compression on the other.
Polar section modulus: Z<sub>p</sub> = π × 40³/16 = 12,566 mm³. Torsional shear stress: τ = 450,000/12,566 = 35.81 MPa at the surface.
Signs at the surface: on the bending-compression side the normal stresses add, −23.87 − 95.49 = −119.36 MPa; on the tension side 95.49 − 23.87 = +71.62 MPa. The shear stress 35.81 MPa acts on both.
examples.answer: Direct stress 23.87 MPa (compression), maximum bending stress 95.49 MPa, maximum torsional shear 35.81 MPa; the combined normal stress is −119.36 MPa on one side and +71.62 MPa on the other.

examples.question: A lever of rectangular section 15 mm wide and 45 mm deep is pushed by a 1.2 kN force at 300 mm from its pivot. The pivot pin is 20 mm in diameter and carries 30 kN in double shear. Find the bending stress in the lever at the pivot, the maximum transverse shear stress in the lever and the shear stress in the pin.
steps: Bending moment at the pivot: M = 1200 × 300 = 360,000 N·mm.
Z = bh²/6 = 15 × 45²/6 = 5062.5 mm³. Bending stress σ<sub>b</sub> = 360,000/5062.5 = 71.1 MPa.
Transverse shear in the lever: V = 1200 N, A = 15 × 45 = 675 mm², τ<sub>max</sub> = 1.5 × 1200/675 = 2.67 MPa, about 4 % of the bending stress.
Pin in double shear: A = 2 × π × 20²/4 = 628.3 mm²; τ = 30,000/628.3 = 47.7 MPa.
examples.answer: Lever: σ<sub>b</sub> = 71.1 MPa, transverse shear 2.67 MPa (negligible). Pin: τ = 47.7 MPa.

traps: Using d instead of d/2 for the outer fibre, or the diameter instead of the radius in τ = Tr/J.
Adding bending (normal) stress and torsional (shear) stress as if they were the same kind; combine them through principal stresses.
Using I in the torsion formula or J in the bending formula; for a solid circle J = 2I.
Forgetting that a pin in a fork is in double shear (twice the area).
Putting M in N·m and y in mm in one formula: convert M to N·mm so that the stress comes out in N/mm² (MPa); leaving M in N·m gives a stress 1000 times too small.

quiz.q: Write the section modulus of a rectangle and of a solid circle.
quiz.a: Rectangle: Z = bh²/6. Solid circle: Z = πd³/32.

quiz.q: State three assumptions of the bending formula σ = My/I.
quiz.a: Linear elastic material obeying Hooke's law; small deflection; plane sections remain plane (the beam is initially straight).

quiz.q: Why is the bending stress zero at the neutral axis?
quiz.a: In σ = My/I, y = 0 there: the fibres at the neutral axis neither stretch nor shorten.

quiz.q: Why is a hollow shaft lighter than a solid one of the same torsional strength?
quiz.a: Shear stress is largest at the surface and small near the axis, so the core carries little torque. Removing it saves much mass and little J.

quiz.q: A solid shaft of 50 mm diameter carries a bending moment of 800 N·m. Find the maximum bending stress.
A 30 mm solid shaft carries a torque of 300 N·m. Find the maximum shear stress.
For the same solid shaft and M = T numerically, which stress is larger and by what ratio?
quiz.a: σ = 32M/(πd³) and τ = 16T/(πd³), so σ/τ = 2: the bending stress is twice the shear stress.

beyond: These hand formulas feed shaft-sizing spreadsheets and are the first check on any finite element model: if FEA disagrees with My/I away from holes and loads, the model is wrong. For thin-walled and open sections (channels, angles) torsion and bending couple through the shear centre. Search next for shear centre, thin-walled torsion and stress concentration factors.

figure.caption: How each load spreads across the diameter of the 40 mm shaft in the first worked example. The axial load gives a uniform 23.87 MPa compression, bending a linear stress from +95.49 to −95.49 MPa through zero at the neutral axis, and torsion a shear stress from zero at the axis to 35.81 MPa at the surface.
